title: The de-intellectualisation of teaching
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes argues that teaching, one of the most intellectually demanding professions, is increasingly flattened into the performance of approved moves - cold call, model, exit ticket - severed from the professional thought that should underpin them, drawing on Sam Gibbs's Tes argument that accountability pressures have sacrificed teachers' intellectual process and professional curiosity. She tells the story of a senior leader designing CPD for their 'thickest teacher', arguing this single phrase reveals a leadership culture built on contempt that impoverishes the whole staff, not just its target. Her central claim is that 'the strategy is not the pedagogy - the decision is the pedagogy', and that a profession becomes de-intellectualised when its members are not trusted to understand the why behind their practice. She closes by reframing the questions leaders should ask in CPD design, from 'how do we make this simple enough for the weakest teacher?' to 'how do we make the complexity clear enough that every teacher can think with it?'
points: Hughes's central formulation - 'the strategy is not the pedagogy. The decision is the pedagogy' - crystallises her argument that visible technique use is a poor proxy for genuine instructional judgement.
Her anecdote about CPD designed for the 'thickest teacher' illustrates how leadership contempt for one colleague quietly degrades professional culture for everyone, not just the target.

She identifies an irony in the profession: intellectual status often attaches to distance from the classroom, while those doing the most cognitively demanding daily work receive checklists and simplified routines.
Her reframed CPD questions - understanding over compliance, judgement over uniformity - offer leaders a concrete alternative design principle.
quotes: Teaching asks a human being to know a subject deeply, understand how novices encounter it, anticipate misconception, respond to emotion, build culture, sustain attention, interpret evidence, make ethical decisions and adapt in real time.

This teacher, the leader explained, just needs to be told exactly what to do. The CPD, therefore, had to be simple enough that even they could follow it. There, in one sentence, was the whole problem.
The strategy is not the pedagogy. The decision is the pedagogy.
The further some people move from the classroom, the more they are permitted to be complex. The closer teachers are to the work, the more they are asked to be simple.

A profession becomes de-intellectualised when its members are not trusted to understand the why. It becomes re-intellectualised when leaders insist that every teacher, novice or expert, is entitled to the deep structure of the work.
